about: LL141 Introduction to Legal Systems is a compulsory, non-credit-bearing foundation course for first-year LLB in Laws (and BA Anthropology and Law) students at LSE. According to the 2026/27 course guide, it runs as an intensive series of lectures in the first two weeks of Autumn Term, with a Welcome Week session on varieties of legal order, and covers theories of what law is, how judges interpret and develop English law (compared with continental Europe and the US), and how legal institutions have changed. Its material is discussed in the classes for Contract Law, Tort Law, Public Law and Criminal Law. There is a mandatory formative essay of up to 1,500 words written over the December–January vacation, which must be resubmitted in Winter Term if not of a satisfactory standard; the guide lists no exam.
topics: Adjudication and due process: the role of the trial
The judiciary: does it matter who the judges are?
Developments in civil justice and alternative dispute resolution
Legal pluralism: social ordering beyond formal law

notes.body:
The 2026/27 course guide says LL141 begins in Welcome Week with a session on varieties of legal order: civilian and common law systems, and national, sub-national, transnational and international law, approached comparatively and historically. The point is that "the law" in England and Wales is one legal order among many, with its own history.

Common law and civil law traditions
- The common law developed in England after 1066 through the royal courts. Under Henry II (1154–1189) royal justices travelled the country and a law "common" to the realm grew from their decisions. Judges' reasoning in past cases became a central source of law.
- Equity developed in the Court of Chancery to correct the rigidity of the common law. The Judicature Acts 1873–75 merged the courts, so the same courts now apply both.
- The civil law tradition descends from Roman law, especially Justinian's compilation (the Corpus Juris Civilis, 6th century), revived in medieval European universities. Its modern form is codification: the French Code civil (1804) and the German Civil Code (BGB, in force 1900).
- In civil law systems the code is the starting point, judges' decisions are not formally binding precedent, and academic writing (doctrine) has high authority. French law even forbids judges from laying down general rules when deciding cases (Code civil, article 5).
- The contrast is real but often overstated: civil law courts follow settled case law in practice, and much modern English law is statute.

The United Kingdom's legal orders
- The UK has three legal jurisdictions: England and Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland. Scots law is a "mixed" system with civilian and common law roots.
- Devolution (Scotland Act 1998, Government of Wales Act 1998 and 2006, Northern Ireland Act 1998) created sub-national legislatures that make law within limits.
- The UK has no single codified constitution. Parliament is sovereign: courts cannot strike down Acts of Parliament, though they can declare them incompatible with Convention rights under the Human Rights Act 1998, s 4.

Comparison with the United States
The US is also a common law system, but with a written federal constitution and judicial review of legislation (Marbury v Madison (1803)). The US Supreme Court can strike down statutes and has overruled its own major precedents (e.g. Brown v Board of Education (1954) overruling Plessy v Ferguson (1896)). This makes the politics of judicial appointment much more visible than in the UK.

International and transnational law
- International law governs relations between states. Its sources are listed in Article 38(1) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice: treaties, international custom, general principles of law, and (as subsidiary means) judicial decisions and the teachings of leading writers.
- The European Convention on Human Rights (a Council of Europe treaty, not EU law) takes effect in UK law through the Human Rights Act 1998.
- The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, with the transition period ending on 31 December 2020. EU-derived law kept in force by the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 was renamed "assimilated law" from 1 January 2024 by the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023.
- Transnational orders include rules made by private or hybrid bodies, such as international commercial arbitration and sports governing bodies, which regulate conduct across borders without being national law.

Why it matters for LL141
Later topics (precedent, interpretation, pluralism) all ask how English law compares with other orders and how its institutions have changed over time.

Exam tips: in essays, use at least one comparison (civil law, US, or international) to show that English arrangements are a choice, not a necessity.

LL141 introduces the main theories of what law is. The 2026/27 reading includes Lon Fuller's "The Case of the Speluncean Explorers" (1949), David Dyzenhaus on "The Grudge Informer Case Revisited" (2008), Nicola Lacey's biography of H L A Hart (2004) and Tom Bingham's The Rule of Law (2010).

Legal positivism
Positivists say that whether a rule is law depends on its source in social facts, not on its moral merit.
- John Austin, The Province of Jurisprudence Determined (1832): law is a command of a sovereign (someone habitually obeyed who does not habitually obey anyone else), backed by a sanction.
- H L A Hart, The Concept of Law (1961), criticised Austin: many laws confer powers (to make contracts, wills or marriages) rather than command; law persists when sovereigns change; and legislators are bound by their own laws. The command model is "the gunman situation writ large".
- Hart's alternative: law is a union of primary rules (which govern conduct) and secondary rules: a rule of recognition (identifying valid law), rules of change and rules of adjudication. Officials must accept the rule of recognition from an "internal point of view".
- Hans Kelsen, Pure Theory of Law, traced the validity of every norm back to a presupposed basic norm (Grundnorm).

Natural law
Natural lawyers say law's identity is connected to morality or reason. The idea that a sufficiently unjust law is not truly law runs from Augustine and Aquinas to modern writers such as John Finnis (Natural Law and Natural Rights, 1980).
- Gustav Radbruch, after Nazi rule, argued (1946) that statutes whose injustice reaches an intolerable degree should give way to justice.

The Hart–Fuller debate (1958)
- In the Harvard Law Review, Hart defended the separation of law and morals; Lon Fuller replied that law has an inner morality.
- Their example was the "grudge informer": a woman who, in 1944, denounced her husband to the Nazi authorities for remarks critical of Hitler, and was prosecuted after the war. Hart thought it more honest to admit that the Nazi law was law but should not be obeyed, or to punish by retrospective statute; Fuller thought a regime so lawless did not deserve the name of law. Dyzenhaus (2008) revisits what the German court actually decided.
- Fuller's The Morality of Law (1964) sets out eight requirements for a legal system: rules must be general, publicised, prospective, clear, consistent, possible to comply with, reasonably stable, and applied by officials as declared.

Interpretivism
Ronald Dworkin (Taking Rights Seriously, 1977; Law's Empire, 1986) argued that law includes principles as well as rules, and that judges must find the interpretation that best fits and justifies the legal record. His example, Riggs v Palmer (New York, 1889), stopped a murderer inheriting under his victim's will.

The Speluncean Explorers
Fuller's imaginary case has trapped explorers who kill and eat one of their party to survive. Five judges of the "Supreme Court of Newgarth" give opinions ranging from strict literalism to natural law to common sense and public opinion. The court is evenly divided, so the convictions stand. It is a compact way to compare theories of law and of judging.

The rule of law
Bingham's The Rule of Law (2010) proposes eight principles, including that law should be accessible, clear and predictable; questions of right should be decided by law, not discretion; the law should apply equally to all; and the state should comply with its international obligations.

Exam tips: be precise about what positivism claims (identification of law, not approval of it), and use the Speluncean Explorers or the grudge informer as worked examples.

Most law today is statute, so a core question is how judges in England and Wales read it. The 2026/27 course guide also asks how English judicial interpretation compares with continental Europe and the United States.

Traditional "rules"
- Literal rule: give words their ordinary meaning even if the result is odd. In Whiteley v Chappell (1868) LR 4 QB 147 a man who impersonated a dead voter was acquitted because a dead person was not "entitled to vote". In Fisher v Bell [1961] 1 QB 394 a flick knife in a shop window was not "offered for sale", because in contract law a display is an invitation to treat.
- Golden rule: depart from the ordinary meaning to avoid absurdity or repugnance (Grey v Pearson (1857) 6 HLC 61). In Adler v George [1964] 2 QB 7, "in the vicinity of" a prohibited place was read to include being inside it. In Re Sigsworth [1935] Ch 89 a son who murdered his mother could not inherit from her under the intestacy rules.
- Mischief rule (Heydon's Case (1584)): ask what mischief the statute was meant to remedy. In Smith v Hughes [1960] 1 WLR 830 prostitutes soliciting from windows and balconies were "in a street". In Royal College of Nursing v DHSS [1981] AC 800 the House of Lords (3–2) held that nurses could carry out parts of medically induced abortions under the Abortion Act 1967, as the Act's purpose was to ensure abortions were done safely in hospital under a doctor's responsibility.

The modern approach: text in context, read purposively
- The courts now speak less of separate "rules" and more of a single search for the meaning of the words in their context and in light of the statute's purpose.
- R (Quintavalle) v Secretary of State for Health [2003] UKHL 13: the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990 was read purposively to cover embryos created by cell nuclear replacement, a technique unknown when it was passed.
- R (O) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2022] UKSC 3: Lord Hodge said the words Parliament chose, read in context, are the primary source of meaning; external aids (explanatory notes, Law Commission reports, White Papers) are secondary and cannot displace clear words that make sense in context.
- Courts may correct an obvious drafting error if they are sure of the intended purpose, that Parliament failed to give effect to it by inadvertence, and of the substance of the provision Parliament would have made (Inco Europe Ltd v First Choice Distribution [2000] 1 WLR 586).

Aids and presumptions
- Hansard: Pepper v Hart [1993] AC 593 allows reference to clear ministerial statements where legislation is ambiguous, obscure or leads to absurdity.
- The Interpretation Act 1978 supplies default meanings (e.g. the singular includes the plural).
- Presumptions include the principle of legality: fundamental rights cannot be overridden by general words (R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex p Simms [2000] 2 AC 115, Lord Hoffmann).

The Human Rights Act 1998
- Section 3: so far as possible, legislation must be read and given effect compatibly with Convention rights. This can require a strained reading: in Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza [2004] UKHL 30 a same-sex partner was treated as living with the tenant "as his or her wife or husband".
- Section 4: if a compatible reading is impossible, higher courts may make a declaration of incompatibility, which does not affect the statute's validity.

Comparative points
Continental courts and the Court of Justice of the EU have long used purposive (teleological) reasoning. In the US, debates between textualists and purposivists are sharp and closely tied to constitutional politics.

Exam tips: avoid treating the literal, golden and mischief rules as a fixed menu; explain how the modern contextual and purposive approach absorbs them, and use HRA s 3 to show interpretation shaped by rights.

The common law is made and developed by judges through precedent (stare decisis): later courts follow earlier decisions on the same legal point. LL141's 2026/27 reading includes Philip Sales, "The Common Law: Context and Method" (2019), and R (Youngsam) v Parole Board [2019] EWCA Civ 229, especially Leggatt LJ at paragraphs 58–59.

Ratio and obiter
- Only the ratio decidendi (the legal reasoning necessary for the decision) binds. Obiter dicta (other remarks) can only persuade.
- In Youngsam, Leggatt LJ explained that the ratio is found from the court's rulings and reasons, read against the facts and issues. He listed factors bearing on how far a later court may assess an earlier ruling's persuasiveness, including how far the judges agreed, how clear the reasoning was, whether the point was argued, whether earlier authorities were considered, whether later cases approved it, whether it has been criticised, and the relative status of the two courts.
- Distinguishing: a later court can refuse to follow a precedent if the material facts differ. This is a main source of flexibility.

The hierarchy in England and Wales
- The Supreme Court (replacing the Appellate Committee of the House of Lords from 2009 under the Constitutional Reform Act 2005) binds all lower courts.
- The House of Lords' Practice Statement (Judicial Precedent) [1966] 1 WLR 1234 allowed it to depart from its own decisions "when it appears right to do so". The Supreme Court applies the same approach (e.g. Knauer v Ministry of Justice [2016] UKSC 9; R v Jogee [2016] UKSC 8, correcting a wrong turn in the law of complicity). Examples of quick departures include R v Shivpuri [1987] AC 1 overruling Anderton v Ryan [1985] AC 560.
- The Court of Appeal (Civil Division) is bound by its own decisions, subject to the exceptions in Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co [1944] KB 718: conflicting Court of Appeal decisions; a decision that cannot stand with a later House of Lords or Supreme Court decision; and decisions given per incuriam. The Criminal Division has slightly more flexibility where liberty is at stake.
- The High Court is bound by the Supreme Court and Court of Appeal.
- Privy Council decisions are normally only persuasive, but in Willers v Joyce (No 2) [2016] UKSC 44 the Supreme Court held that the Privy Council can expressly direct domestic courts to treat its decision as stating English law, since its panels are usually Supreme Court justices.

Do judges make law?
- The old "declaratory theory" said judges only find existing law. Lord Reid called this a "fairy tale" ("The Judge as Law Maker", 1972).
- Examples of judicial development: R v R [1992] 1 AC 599 removed the marital rape exemption; Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562 created the modern law of negligence.
- Because judicial change is retrospective, courts are cautious where Parliament is better placed, for example on policy issues requiring consultation.

Comparisons
- Civil law courts are not formally bound by precedent, though settled case law (jurisprudence constante in France) is highly persuasive.
- The US Supreme Court overrules its own precedents more openly and politically, for example Dobbs v Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022) overruling Roe v Wade (1973).

Evaluation
- For precedent: certainty, equality (like cases treated alike), efficiency.
- Against: rigidity, slow change, dependence on the chance of litigation, and complexity from huge volumes of case law.

Exam tips: identify the court and its place in the hierarchy before deciding whether a precedent binds; then consider whether it can be distinguished or departed from.

This topic asks what trials are for and how far the reality of justice matches the ideal. The 2026/27 reading includes The Secret Barrister's Stories of the Law and How It's Broken (2018), a critical account of the criminal courts.

What is adjudication?
- Adjudication is deciding a dispute by applying law to facts, after both sides have presented proofs and arguments to an impartial decision-maker.
- Lon Fuller, "The Forms and Limits of Adjudication" (published 1978), argued that adjudication is suited to deciding claims of right but struggles with "polycentric" problems with many interconnected consequences, such as allocating budgets.

Adversarial and inquisitorial models
- England and Wales use an adversarial model: the parties gather and present evidence and the judge acts as umpire, with juries deciding facts in serious criminal cases.
- Many civil law systems are more inquisitorial: a judge or investigating magistrate takes a more active role in finding the facts.
- Each model has strengths: party control and testing of evidence through cross-examination versus thorough official investigation and less dependence on the quality of lawyers.

Due process values
- The presumption of innocence and the burden on the prosecution to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt (Woolmington v DPP [1935] AC 462).
- Article 6 ECHR: a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal.
- Open justice: courts sit in public except where strictly necessary (Scott v Scott [1913] AC 417).
- Impartiality: "justice should not only be done, but should manifestly and undoubtedly be seen to be done" (R v Sussex Justices, ex p McCarthy [1924] 1 KB 256, Lord Hewart CJ). The test for apparent bias is whether a fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias (Porter v Magill [2001] UKHL 67). A judge with a financial interest in a party is automatically disqualified, without any inquiry into actual or apparent bias (Dimes v Grand Junction Canal (1852) 3 HLC 759, where the Lord Chancellor held shares in a party); the same applies where the judge is closely linked to a party promoting a cause in the case (R v Bow Street Magistrate, ex p Pinochet Ugarte (No 2) [2000] 1 AC 119).
- Hearing the other side: oral hearings matter where facts are disputed or fairness requires it (Osborn v Parole Board [2013] UKSC 61).

Herbert Packer's two models
Packer (1964) contrasted a "crime control" model, valuing speedy and efficient processing of the guilty, with a "due process" model, which puts obstacles in the way of the state to protect the innocent and limit state power. Most systems mix the two.

The vanishing trial
- Most criminal cases end in guilty pleas, encouraged by sentencing credit of up to one third for an early plea. Most civil disputes settle or are resolved without trial.
- Marc Galanter's "The Vanishing Trial" (2004) documented this in the US; similar trends exist in England and Wales.
- Critics worry about pressure on defendants to plead and the loss of public norm-setting; defenders point to cost, speed and the wishes of the parties.

Current developments
Crown Court backlogs led to the Independent Review of the Criminal Courts (led by Sir Brian Leveson) and then to the Courts and Tribunals Bill. As brought to the House of Lords, the Bill would remove an adult defendant's right to elect Crown Court trial in either-way cases, extend magistrates' sentencing powers and introduce judge-only trials for certain complex and lengthy cases. A provision for a Crown Court "bench division", which would have tried some either-way offences without a jury, was removed during the Bill's Commons passage. At the time of writing (October 2026) the Bill is in the House of Lords (second reading 27 October 2026); check its progress, as the details may change.

Exam tips: tie due process values to specific rules (burden of proof, Article 6, bias tests) and ask how far guilty pleas, settlement and delay undermine the ideal of the trial.

notes.h: The judiciary: does it matter who the judges are?
notes.body:
This topic asks whether the identity of judges matters for the legitimacy and content of the law. The 2026/27 reading includes Alexandra Wilson's In Black and White (2020), a young barrister's account of race and class in the justice system, and Rosemary Hunter, "More than just a different face? Judicial diversity and decision-making" (2015).

Judicial independence
- Judges of the senior courts hold office during good behaviour and can be removed only by the Crown on an address of both Houses of Parliament (originally the Act of Settlement 1701; now the Senior Courts Act 1981, s 11(3)).
- The Constitutional Reform Act 2005 requires ministers to uphold the continued independence of the judiciary (s 3), reformed the office of Lord Chancellor, and created the Supreme Court (in operation from October 2009).
- The mandatory retirement age for judges was raised from 70 to 75 by the Public Service Pensions and Judicial Offices Act 2022.

Appointments
- The Judicial Appointments Commission, created under the 2005 Act, selects candidates for courts in England and Wales. Selection must be solely on merit (s 63(2)), and the candidate must be of good character.
- Since amendments by the Crime and Courts Act 2013, where two candidates are of equal merit, a preference may be given to increase diversity (the "tie-breaker", linked to s 159 Equality Act 2010).
- Supreme Court justices are chosen by ad hoc selection commissions.

Why diversity might matter
- Legitimacy and public confidence: a judiciary drawn from a narrow group may not command trust, especially in communities that already feel badly treated by the justice system.
- Fairness of opportunity: talented lawyers from under-represented groups should have equal chances of appointment.
- Decision-making: different life experiences may affect how judges find facts, assess credibility or frame legal questions. Feminist judgments projects, where scholars rewrite real judgments from a feminist perspective, explore this. Hunter (2015) reviews the research and finds the evidence on whether judges from under-represented groups decide differently to be mixed, with any differences depending on context; she stresses that the case for diversity does not rest on outcomes alone.
- Counter-arguments: judges are trained to apply law impartially, and individual judges do not "represent" a group; differences in outcomes may be small or hard to measure.

Who are the judges?
- Judicial diversity statistics are published annually. They show that women and people from ethnic minority backgrounds remain under-represented, especially in the senior judiciary, though representation has risen over time. Check the latest figures rather than relying on older numbers.
- Lady Hale became the first female Law Lord (2004) and the first female President of the Supreme Court (2017).

The politics of the judiciary
- J A G Griffith, The Politics of the Judiciary (1977), argued that senior judges' shared background led them to favour established interests.
- Judges' growing role in high-profile public law cases (for example R (Miller) v Prime Minister [2019] UKSC 41, on prorogation) has led to arguments about whether judges are drawn into politics, and some critics now ask whether appointments should involve more political scrutiny. Others argue that independence requires keeping politics out of appointments.

Comparison with the United States
US federal judges are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, so appointments are openly political. The UK system aims to avoid this, at the cost of less public scrutiny.

Exam tips: distinguish clearly between arguments from legitimacy, equality of opportunity and difference in decision-making; support claims about outcomes with evidence or acknowledge where evidence is limited.

Civil justice concerns how private disputes (contract, tort, property, family and many claims against public bodies) are resolved. A recurring theme is that most disputes never reach a judge, and that the state has increasingly pushed them towards other methods.

The Woolf reforms
- Lord Woolf's Access to Justice reports (1995 interim, 1996 final) diagnosed civil litigation as too expensive, too slow and too complex.
- They led to the Civil Procedure Rules 1998 (in force April 1999), with an "overriding objective" of dealing with cases justly and at proportionate cost (CPR 1.1), active case management by judges, pre-action protocols and different "tracks" for different claims.

Costs and legal aid
- Lord Justice Jackson's Review of Civil Litigation Costs (final report published in January 2010) led to changes in costs rules and funding arrangements, many implemented in 2013.
- The Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012 removed legal aid from many areas of civil law, increasing the number of litigants in person.
- In R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor [2017] UKSC 51 the Supreme Court held that employment tribunal fees were unlawful because they prevented access to justice, stressing that courts serve the public, not just the parties.

Alternative dispute resolution (ADR)
ADR covers methods other than court adjudication:
- Negotiation between the parties.
- Mediation: a neutral third party helps the parties reach their own agreement; it is voluntary and confidential, and the mediator does not impose a result.
- Arbitration: a private, binding decision by an arbitrator chosen under an agreement, governed in England and Wales by the Arbitration Act 1996.
- Ombudsmen and tribunals also resolve many disputes outside the ordinary courts.

From encouraging to requiring ADR
- Halsey v Milton Keynes General NHS Trust [2004] EWCA Civ 576 suggested that courts could not compel unwilling parties to mediate, though unreasonable refusal could be penalised in costs.
- Churchill v Merthyr Tydfil County Borough Council [2023] EWCA Civ 1416 held that Halsey's remarks on compulsion were obiter, and that courts can order parties to engage in a non-court dispute resolution process, or stay proceedings for it, provided the order does not impair the very essence of the right to a judicial hearing, pursues the legitimate aim of settling the dispute fairly, quickly and at reasonable cost, and is proportionate to that aim.
- From 1 October 2024 the CPR were amended so that the overriding objective expressly includes promoting or using ADR, courts can order parties to engage in ADR, and failure to comply or unreasonable refusal can be taken into account on costs.
- Since May 2024, most specified money claims on the small claims track have been automatically referred to a free one-hour telephone mediation run by HMCTS.

Digital justice
The Civil Courts Structure Review (Briggs LJ, 2016) proposed an online court for lower-value claims. The Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 created an Online Procedure Rule Committee to make rules for online procedures.

Debates
- For ADR: cheaper, quicker, less adversarial, and gives the parties control.
- Against: power imbalances between parties, private outcomes that do not develop the law, and the risk that "access to justice" becomes access to a cheaper substitute. Hazel Genn (Judging Civil Justice, her 2008 Hamlyn Lectures) argued that the decline of civil adjudication weakens the public role of courts in making and declaring law.

Exam tips: present the reforms as a story (Woolf, Jackson, LASPO, Churchill, 2024 rules) and evaluate them against access to justice and the public value of adjudication.

Legal pluralism is the idea that more than one normative order operates in the same social field. It challenges the assumption that law means only state law. The 2026/27 reading includes Abdullahi An-Na'im, "The Compatibility Dialectic" (2010), on how Islamic law and state law can legitimately coexist.

Key ideas
- Eugen Ehrlich (Fundamental Principles of the Sociology of Law, 1913) distinguished the "living law" that actually governs social life from the law in codes and court decisions.
- John Griffiths, "What is Legal Pluralism?" (1986), distinguished "weak" (or juristic) pluralism, where the state recognises other bodies of law (e.g. personal or religious law in some colonial and post-colonial states), from "strong" pluralism, the empirical fact that many normative orders coexist whether or not the state recognises them.
- Sally Falk Moore (1973) described "semi-autonomous social fields": groups (such as a garment industry or a workplace) that generate their own rules and enforcement but are also open to outside law.
- Sally Engle Merry, "Legal Pluralism" (1988), surveyed the field and showed how colonial and modern societies combine state and non-state orders.

Ordering without (state) law
- Stewart Macaulay, "Non-Contractual Relations in Business" (1963): many businesses rarely rely on formal contract law to plan or resolve disputes, preferring relationships and reputation.
- Robert Ellickson, Order without Law (1991): ranchers in Shasta County, California, settled cattle-trespass disputes by informal norms of neighbourliness, often ignoring the formal law.
- These studies show social order can be maintained by norms outside law, and they raise questions about when state law is needed at all.

Religious and community normative orders in England and Wales
- Religious tribunals such as the Beth Din can act as arbitrators for commercial disputes under the Arbitration Act 1996, if the parties agree; their decisions are then enforceable like other awards, subject to the Act's safeguards.
- Sharia councils mainly deal with religious divorces (almost all users are women seeking an Islamic divorce) and have no legal power under English law. An independent review published by the Home Office in February 2018, chaired by Mona Siddiqui, found evidence of both good and bad practice, including practices that discriminate against women, such as women being asked to make concessions to their husbands to obtain a divorce. It recommended changing marriage law so that a civil marriage is registered before or at the same time as an Islamic ceremony, awareness campaigns about women's legal rights, and (by a majority of the panel) a body to set a code of practice for councils. The government rejected the regulation proposal, stating that sharia law has no jurisdiction in the UK.
- The debate is between respect for religious and community autonomy, and protecting vulnerable members, especially women, from unequal treatment and from being denied the protection of state law. An-Na'im argues that Islamic law cannot be enforced as state law, but keeps its religious authority for believers outside the state's legal system; the two can coexist and influence each other as complementary systems, and Islamic principles can enter public debate only through 'civic reason' that all citizens can engage with.

Global and transnational pluralism
- International law, regional human rights systems and transnational private regimes (commercial arbitration, sports bodies, internet governance) operate alongside national law.
- Some writers describe a global legal pluralism in which no single legal order is supreme, raising questions about legitimacy and accountability.

Critiques
- Defining "law" broadly risks calling every social rule law, losing what is distinctive about legal orders (a point positivists such as Hart would press).
- Pluralism can be used to justify leaving oppressive community norms unchallenged.

Exam tips: define legal pluralism precisely (weak vs strong), give at least one empirical study (Macaulay or Ellickson) and one English example (religious tribunals), and connect to the "what is law?" debate.

England and Wales involve non-lawyers in deciding cases more than many legal systems: juries in the Crown Court and lay magistrates in the magistrates' courts. The 2026/27 reading includes the LSE/Guardian Reading the Riots study (2011) and The Lammy Review: Final Report (2017).

Juries
- Juries of 12 try contested indictable cases in the Crown Court. Jurors are chosen at random from the electoral register; they must be aged 18 to 75 (Juries Act 1974, s 1, as amended by the Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015).
- Verdicts should be unanimous, but after at least two hours of deliberation a judge can accept a majority verdict of 11–1 or 10–2 (Juries Act 1974, s 17).
- Deliberations are secret: it is an offence to disclose them (Juries Act 1974, s 20D) and for jurors to research the case (s 20A); the House of Lords upheld the common law secrecy rule in R v Mirza [2004] UKHL 2.
- Jury independence has deep roots: Bushell's Case (1670) held that jurors could not be punished for their verdict. Juries sometimes acquit against the evidence on grounds of conscience, as in R v Ponting [1985] Crim LR 318, where a civil servant who leaked documents was acquitted despite the judge's direction.
- Patrick Devlin (Trial by Jury, 1956) called the jury "the lamp that shows that freedom lives".

Arguments for and against juries
- For: democratic participation, public confidence, community standards (e.g. in judging dishonesty), and a check on oppressive laws or prosecutions.
- Against: cost and delay, the difficulty of long and complex cases (especially fraud), no reasons given, risk of prejudice, and jury tampering.
- Evidence: Cheryl Thomas's research for the Ministry of Justice (Are Juries Fair?, 2010) found little evidence of unfairness by ethnicity in jury verdicts. The Lammy Review drew on her analysis to call juries "a success story" of the justice system, finding that juries, including all-white juries, did not deliver different results for ethnic minority and white defendants.

Limits on jury trial
- Most criminal cases are tried in magistrates' courts, so juries decide a small share of cases.
- A judge-only trial can be ordered where there is evidence of a real and present danger of jury tampering and the risk is so substantial, despite any protective steps, that trial without a jury is necessary in the interests of justice (Criminal Justice Act 2003, s 44). The Court of Appeal ordered such a trial in R v Twomey [2009] EWCA Crim 1035, an armed robbery case.
- The Courts and Tribunals Bill would remove the right of adult defendants to elect Crown Court trial in either-way cases and introduce judge-only trials for certain complex and lengthy cases. A Crown Court bench division, which would have tried some either-way offences without a jury, was removed during the Bill's Commons passage. At the time of writing (October 2026) the Bill is in the House of Lords (second reading 27 October 2026); check its progress.

Lay magistrates
- Lay magistrates (justices of the peace) are unpaid volunteers who usually sit in benches of two or three, advised on law by a legally qualified adviser. District judges (magistrates' courts) are paid professional judges.
- Magistrates decide guilt and sentence in summary cases and many either-way cases.
- For: local knowledge, community involvement, low cost. Against: concerns about consistency, case-hardening and limited diversity.

Other lay participation
Lay members sit with employment judges in some employment tribunal hearings, and specialist lay members sit in other tribunals.

Connecting to other topics
Lay participation links to adjudication (who finds facts), the judiciary (diversity and legitimacy) and the rule of law (accountability to the community).

Exam tips: weigh democratic and legitimacy arguments against efficiency, and support claims about jury fairness with Thomas's research and the Lammy Review rather than assumption.

cards.b: Law developed by judges' decisions in the royal courts after 1066, with precedent central; equity developed alongside in Chancery; courts merged by the Judicature Acts 1873-75.
Descends from Roman law (Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis); modern codes such as the French Code civil (1804) and German BGB (1900) are the primary source.
Three: England and Wales; Scotland (a mixed civil/common law system); and Northern Ireland.
Article 38(1) ICJ Statute: treaties, international custom, general principles of law; judicial decisions and leading writers as subsidiary means.
EU-derived law retained after Brexit, renamed 'assimilated law' from 1 January 2024 by the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023.
US Supreme Court case establishing judicial review of legislation; contrast UK parliamentary sovereignty (only declarations of incompatibility under HRA s 4).
The view that whether a norm is law depends on its social source (e.g. enactment, acceptance by officials), not its moral merit.
Law is a command of a sovereign (habitually obeyed, obeying no one) backed by a sanction (The Province of Jurisprudence Determined, 1832).
A secondary rule, accepted by officials from the internal point of view, that sets the criteria for identifying valid law (The Concept of Law, 1961).
Eight requirements: general, publicised, prospective, clear, consistent, possible to obey, stable, and congruence between declared rules and official action (1964).
Statute must give way to justice where its injustice reaches an intolerable degree (Radbruch, 1946, responding to Nazi law).
Imaginary case: trapped explorers kill and eat a companion; five judges reason in different ways; evenly divided court leaves convictions standing.
Law includes principles (e.g. no one should profit from their own wrong, Riggs v Palmer 1889) which judges weigh; the right answer best fits and justifies the law.
Give words their ordinary meaning even if the result seems odd (Whiteley v Chappell, 1868; Fisher v Bell, 1961).
Depart from ordinary meaning to avoid absurdity or repugnance (Grey v Pearson, 1857; Adler v George, 1964; Re Sigsworth, 1935).
Interpret the statute to suppress the mischief it was passed to remedy (Smith v Hughes, 1960; RCN v DHSS, 1981).
Hansard may be used where legislation is ambiguous, obscure or absurd, and a minister's statement is clear on the point.
Statutory words read in context are the primary source of meaning; external aids are secondary and cannot displace clear words.
So far as possible, legislation must be read and given effect compatibly with Convention rights (e.g. Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza, 2004).
Fundamental rights cannot be overridden by general or ambiguous words; Parliament must squarely confront what it is doing.
The legal reasoning necessary for the decision on the material facts; the only binding part of a judgment.
Remarks not necessary for the decision (e.g. hypotheticals, wider statements); persuasive only.
House of Lords may depart from its own decisions when it appears right to do so; applies to the Supreme Court (e.g. Knauer, 2016).
Court of Appeal bound by its own decisions except: conflicting CA decisions; inconsistent later HL/UKSC decision; per incuriam.
Privy Council decisions are normally persuasive, but the Board can expressly direct that its ruling states English law.
Declining to follow a precedent because the material facts of the present case are different.
Leggatt LJ: ratio found from rulings and reasons read against facts and issues; listed factors for how far a later court can assess an earlier ruling.
Parties investigate and present evidence; judge acts as neutral umpire; evidence tested by cross-examination. Contrast inquisitorial systems with active judicial fact-finding.
The 'golden thread': the prosecution must prove the defendant's guilt; the burden does not shift to the accused (subject to insanity and statutory exceptions).
Apparent bias test: would a fair-minded and informed observer conclude there was a real possibility that the tribunal was biased?
HL set aside its own earlier decision because Lord Hoffmann had links to Amnesty International, which had intervened in the appeal: automatic disqualification, with no need to show actual bias.
Crime control (efficient processing, presumption of guilt in practice) vs due process (obstacles protecting the innocent and limiting state power).
Problems with many interlocking consequences that adjudication, focused on two-party claims of right, handles poorly.
Senior judges hold office during good behaviour; removable only by the Crown on an address of both Houses (Act of Settlement 1701; Senior Courts Act 1981 s 11(3)).
Created the Supreme Court (from 2009) and the Judicial Appointments Commission; s 3 duty to uphold judicial independence; appointment solely on merit (s 63).
Where candidates are of equal merit, a preference may be given to increase judicial diversity (added by the Crime and Courts Act 2013, linked to s 159 Equality Act 2010).

cards.f: Griffith, The Politics of the Judiciary (1977)
cards.b: Argued senior judges' narrow social background led them to favour established interests and conventional views of the public interest.
75, raised from 70 by the Public Service Pensions and Judicial Offices Act 2022.
Legitimacy and public confidence; equal opportunity; possibly different perspectives in fact-finding and reasoning (debated).
Enabling the court to deal with cases justly and at proportionate cost; since October 2024 expressly includes promoting or using ADR.
Access to Justice reports (1995-96): civil litigation too costly, slow and complex; led to the Civil Procedure Rules 1998 and active case management.
Mediation: neutral helps parties agree; no imposed outcome. Arbitration: private binding decision by arbitrator (Arbitration Act 1996).

Halsey: courts should not compel mediation (remarks later held obiter). Churchill: courts can order ADR if it does not impair the essence of the right to a hearing, pursues a legitimate aim and is proportionate.
Employment tribunal fees unlawful because they prevented access to justice; courts serve a public, not just private, function.
Removed civil legal aid from many areas, increasing the number of litigants in person.
The coexistence of more than one normative order (state law and others such as religious, customary or private orders) in the same social field.
Weak: the state recognises other bodies of law. Strong: many normative orders exist as a social fact, whether or not the state recognises them.
The norms that actually govern social life, as opposed to the formal law of codes and courts (1913).
A social group that makes and enforces its own rules but remains open to outside law and pressure.
Businesses often avoid formal contract law in planning and disputes, relying instead on relationships and reputation.
Shasta County ranchers resolved cattle-trespass disputes through informal neighbourly norms rather than formal law.
After at least two hours' deliberation, a judge may accept 11-1 or 10-2 (Juries Act 1974 s 17).
18 to 75 (Juries Act 1974 s 1, upper limit raised from 70 by the Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015).
Jurors cannot be punished for their verdict; foundation of jury independence.
Civil servant who leaked documents acquitted despite the judge's direction: example of jury equity/nullification.
Ministry of Justice research finding little evidence of unfairness by ethnicity in jury verdicts.
Unpaid volunteer justices of the peace who usually sit in twos or threes with a legally qualified adviser; decide most criminal cases.

questions.q: Which feature best distinguishes the classic civil law tradition from the common law tradition?
options: The civil law tradition governs private (non-criminal) disputes, whereas the common law tradition governs crime
In civil law systems earlier judicial decisions formally bind later courts, whereas common law systems rely mainly on codes
In civil law systems a comprehensive code is the primary source and judicial decisions are not formally binding precedent
The civil law tradition spread from England through the British Empire, whereas the common law grew from Roman law
questions.why: Codification without a formal doctrine of binding precedent is the core contrast; French law even forbids judges from laying down general rules (Code civil, art 5). Reading 'civil law' as 'non-criminal law' confuses the legal family with the civil/criminal division: both traditions have criminal and private law. Saying civil law judges are bound by precedent while common law systems rely on codes reverses the two traditions. The common law, not the civil law, spread through the British Empire, and it is the civil law tradition that descends from Roman law, so that statement swaps their histories.

questions.q: The European Convention on Human Rights takes effect in UK domestic law mainly through which instrument?
options: The European Communities Act 1972, because the Convention is part of EU law
No Act is needed, because treaties the UK ratifies automatically become part of domestic law
The European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018, which kept the Convention in force after Brexit
The Human Rights Act 1998
questions.why: The ECHR is a Council of Europe treaty, given domestic effect mainly by the Human Rights Act 1998. The European Communities Act 1972 gave effect to EU law; treating the Convention as EU law confuses two separate European legal orders. The UK is dualist, so a ratified treaty does not change domestic law until Parliament legislates, which is why the 1998 Act was needed even though the UK had ratified the Convention in 1951. The 2018 Withdrawal Act dealt with EU law after Brexit; leaving the EU did not affect the UK's position under the ECHR.

questions.q: Explain two differences between the common law and civil law traditions and one reason the contrast can be overstated. (4 marks)
markScheme: Source: civil law starts from codes (Code civil 1804, BGB 1900); common law from judicial decisions plus statute
Precedent: binding precedent (stare decisis) in common law; no formal binding precedent in civil law (e.g. French Code civil art 5)
Style/role of doctrine: academic writing more authoritative in civil law; common law judgments longer and discursive
Overstated: civil law courts follow settled case law in practice; much English law is now statute; convergence through EU/ECHR
questions.modelAnswer: First, the starting point differs: civil law systems such as France and Germany start from comprehensive codes (the Code civil of 1804, the BGB in force from 1900), while the common law grew from judicial decisions, now alongside statute. Second, common law courts apply binding precedent, whereas civil law courts are not formally bound by earlier decisions; French law even forbids judges from laying down general rules (Code civil, art 5). The contrast is overstated because civil law courts in practice follow settled lines of case law, and much modern English law is statutory, so the traditions have converged, partly through European law.

questions.q: Which criticism of Austin's command theory did Hart make in The Concept of Law?
options: Law is whatever judges predict will happen
Law depends on a presupposed basic norm
Many laws confer powers, such as the power to make a will, rather than impose duties backed by sanctions
A rule must conform to morality to be valid law
questions.why: Hart's key objection was that power-conferring rules do not fit the command model. Making legal validity depend on morality is a natural law position, which Hart, a positivist, rejected. Prediction of what courts will do is American legal realism, not Hart. The basic norm is Kelsen's concept.

questions.q: In the Speluncean Explorers, what was the overall outcome?
options: The explorers were pardoned by the court
The court held that natural law required acquittal unanimously
The convictions were quashed by a majority
The court was evenly divided, so the convictions were affirmed
questions.why: One judge withdrew and the others split two-two, so the trial court's conviction stood. A majority to quash is wrong because only two judges favoured reversal. Courts do not grant pardons; the Chief Justice suggested executive clemency. The judges disagreed sharply, so 'unanimously' is wrong.

questions.q: Outline Hart's account of law as the union of primary and secondary rules. (5 marks)
markScheme: Primary rules impose duties/govern conduct
Secondary rules are rules about rules: recognition, change, adjudication
Rule of recognition identifies valid law; accepted by officials from the internal point of view
Secondary rules cure defects of a pre-legal regime: uncertainty, static quality, inefficiency
Contrast with Austin's command theory (power-conferring rules, continuity)
questions.modelAnswer: Hart argued in The Concept of Law (1961) that a legal system combines primary rules, which tell people what they must or must not do, with secondary rules, which are rules about rules. A simple society with only primary rules would suffer three defects: uncertainty about what the rules are, a static set of rules that cannot be changed deliberately, and inefficient enforcement. The rule of recognition cures uncertainty by setting criteria of legal validity; rules of change allow rules to be made or repealed; and rules of adjudication empower officials to decide disputes. The rule of recognition exists because officials accept it from the internal point of view, as a standard they use to criticise and justify. This replaced Austin's model of commands backed by sanctions, which could not explain power-conferring rules or the continuity of law when rulers change.

questions.q: Which case is the standard example of the mischief rule being used to hold that prostitutes soliciting from balconies and windows were soliciting 'in a street'?
options: Fisher v Bell [1961]
Whiteley v Chappell (1868)
Adler v George [1964]
Smith v Hughes [1960]
questions.why: Smith v Hughes applied the mischief of the Street Offences Act 1959 (people being solicited in public). Fisher v Bell is a literal-rule case about a flick knife in a shop window. Whiteley v Chappell is a literal-rule case about impersonating a dead voter. Adler v George applied the golden rule to 'in the vicinity of'.

questions.q: Under s 3 of the Human Rights Act 1998, what must a court do if a statute can be read compatibly with Convention rights?
options: Strike down the statute if it is incompatible
Refer the question to the European Court of Human Rights
Read and give effect to it compatibly, so far as possible, even if that is not its most natural meaning
Apply the literal meaning and make a declaration of incompatibility
questions.why: Section 3 requires a compatible reading so far as possible (Ghaidan). UK courts cannot strike down Acts of Parliament. There is no reference procedure to Strasbourg like the EU preliminary reference. A declaration under s 4 is a last resort when a compatible reading is impossible, not an alternative where one is possible.

questions.q: Explain what the Supreme Court said about the role of external aids in R (O) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2022] UKSC 3. (4 marks)
markScheme: Words Parliament chose, read in context of section and statute as a whole, are primary source
Constitutional reason: citizens must be able to rely on the text
External aids (explanatory notes, Law Commission reports, White Papers) secondary: help identify background, mischief and purpose, and resolve ambiguity
Cannot displace meanings that are clear and not absurd in context
questions.modelAnswer: Lord Hodge held that interpretation looks for the meaning of the words Parliament used, read in context: the section, the group of sections and the statute as a whole. These words are the primary source of meaning, partly because citizens must be able to rely on what an Act says. External aids, such as explanatory notes, Law Commission reports and White Papers, have a secondary role: they can reveal the background, the mischief and the purpose, and can help resolve ambiguity. But they cannot displace a meaning that is clear and makes sense in context without absurdity.

questions.q: The Court of Appeal (Civil Division) faces one of its own earlier decisions that is inconsistent with a later Supreme Court decision. What should it do?
options: Follow its own earlier decision, because it is always bound by itself
Refer the question to the Privy Council
Apply the 1966 Practice Statement to overrule its earlier decision
Decline to follow its earlier decision, under the exceptions in Young v Bristol Aeroplane
questions.why: Young v Bristol Aeroplane lets the Court of Appeal depart from its own decision that cannot stand with a later decision of the highest court. 'Always bound' ignores those exceptions. Referring the question to the Privy Council misreads Willers v Joyce: the Board can direct that its own decision states English law, but English courts cannot refer questions to it. The 1966 Practice Statement applied to the House of Lords (now the Supreme Court), not the Court of Appeal.

questions.q: Which statement about the Supreme Court and its own previous decisions is correct?
options: Its previous decisions are merely persuasive in all cases
It is strictly bound by all House of Lords decisions
It may depart from previous decisions when it appears right to do so, following the 1966 Practice Statement approach
It may depart only with the consent of Parliament
questions.why: The Supreme Court applies the Practice Statement approach (e.g. Knauer; Jogee). Being strictly bound was the House of Lords' position before 1966. Requiring Parliament's consent confuses the court's power over its own precedents with Parliament's separate power to reverse a decision by legislation. 'Merely persuasive' describes the status of, for example, most Privy Council decisions; the Supreme Court treats its own earlier decisions as normally binding and departs from them only rarely.

questions.q: Explain the role of distinguishing in the doctrine of precedent, and why it matters for the development of the common law. (4 marks)
markScheme: Only the ratio binds; it is tied to material facts
Distinguishing: later court identifies material factual difference and declines to apply the precedent
Allows lower courts to avoid unsuitable precedents without overruling
Promotes flexibility but risks fine/artificial distinctions and uncertainty; example (e.g. Balfour v Balfour distinguished in Merritt v Merritt)
questions.modelAnswer: Only the ratio of a case binds, and the ratio is tied to the material facts. A later court can therefore distinguish a precedent by identifying a material difference in the facts and declining to apply it. For example, Balfour v Balfour (1919), where an agreement between spouses living together was not binding, was distinguished in Merritt v Merritt (1970) because the spouses had separated. Distinguishing lets courts, including lower courts that cannot overrule, adapt the law to new situations. The risk is that very fine or artificial distinctions make the law complex and uncertain.

questions.q: A High Court judge hearing a planning challenge owns shares in the developer whose permission is under attack, and has not disclosed this. Which statement is correct?
options: The judge is automatically disqualified because of a financial interest in a party, without any need to show actual or apparent bias
The judge may sit, because any unfairness can be corrected on appeal
The judge may sit unless it is proved that the shareholding actually influenced the decision
The judge may sit, because the principle that justice must be seen to be done (ex p McCarthy) applies only to magistrates' courts
questions.why: A financial interest in a party disqualifies a judge automatically, as the Lord Chancellor's shareholding did in Dimes v Grand Junction Canal (1852), a rule restated in Pinochet (No 2); the court does not ask whether the judge was actually influenced. Requiring proof of actual influence confuses automatic disqualification with actual bias, which the law does not require because it is so hard to prove. Ex p McCarthy arose from a magistrates' court, but the principle that justice must be seen to be done applies to every court and tribunal. An appeal does not cure a hearing before a disqualified judge: the decision is set aside, as the House of Lords did with its own decision in Pinochet.

questions.q: What does Fuller mean by calling some problems 'polycentric'?
options: They involve more than one legal order, such as state law and religious law
They involve many interconnected consequences, so adjudication of two-party claims of right handles them poorly
They are disputes with more than two parties, which courts cannot hear
They are hard cases where the law is unclear, so the judge must make new law
questions.why: Fuller compared polycentric problems to a spider's web: pulling one strand changes the tension across the whole web, so they suit managerial or political decision-making better than adjudication. Reading 'polycentric' as 'many parties' misses Fuller's point: the problem is the many interacting consequences, not the number of litigants, and courts routinely hear multi-party cases. Unclear law in 'hard cases' is the concern of Hart's and Dworkin's debate about judicial discretion, not of polycentricity. Several legal orders operating together is legal pluralism, a different idea.

questions.q: Explain the difference between Packer's crime control and due process models of criminal justice. (4 marks)
markScheme: Crime control: priority on efficient suppression of crime; speed, finality, administrative fact-finding; 'conveyor belt'
Due process: priority on protecting the innocent and limiting state power; formal adjudication; 'obstacle course'
Example rules on each side (guilty plea credit vs burden of proof/exclusion of evidence)
Both are ideal types; real systems mix them
questions.modelAnswer: Herbert Packer (1964) described two value systems in criminal justice. The crime control model prioritises suppressing crime efficiently: it trusts police and prosecutors' fact-finding, values speed and finality, and treats the process like a conveyor belt, with guilty pleas as the normal outcome. The due process model prioritises protecting the innocent and limiting state power: it insists on formal adjudication, strict proof and procedural safeguards, like an obstacle course. Sentencing credit for guilty pleas reflects crime control values; the burden of proof beyond reasonable doubt reflects due process. Packer presented these as ideal types; real systems combine both.

questions.q: Under the Constitutional Reform Act 2005, on what basis must judicial appointments in England and Wales be made?
options: To meet fixed quotas for women and ethnic minority judges
Solely on merit, with a tie-breaker for diversity only where candidates are of equal merit
By the Lord Chancellor's personal choice after confidential consultations with senior judges
By election in the candidate's region
questions.why: Section 63 requires selection solely on merit; since the Crime and Courts Act 2013 a preference to increase diversity may be used only between candidates of equal merit. Appointment by the Lord Chancellor after confidential 'soundings' describes the system the 2005 Act replaced when the Judicial Appointments Commission began work in 2006. Judicial elections exist in some US states, not in England and Wales. Fixed quotas would breach the merit principle; the tie-breaker is much narrower.

questions.q: Which argument for judicial diversity does NOT depend on showing that diverse judges decide cases differently?
options: Diverse judges reach better results in sex discrimination cases
A judiciary reflecting society supports public confidence and gives fair access to judicial careers
Women judges are more lenient in sentencing
Ethnic minority judges assess credibility more accurately
questions.why: Legitimacy and equal opportunity arguments hold whether or not outcomes change. The other three options all rest on claims about different decisions, which is exactly the contested empirical question that Hunter and others examine.

questions.q: Why might it matter who the judges are? Give three distinct arguments and one counter-argument. (5 marks)
markScheme: Legitimacy/public confidence: a judiciary resembling society is more trusted
Equality of opportunity in a public career
Decision-making: experience shapes fact-finding, credibility, framing (feminist judgments projects; Hunter 2015 finds the evidence mixed)
Counter: impartial application of law; judges are not representatives; evidence of different outcomes is limited
Uses accurate institutional detail (merit principle, s 63 CRA 2005; tie-breaker)
questions.modelAnswer: First, legitimacy: courts rely on public confidence, and a judiciary drawn from a narrow social group may struggle to command trust, especially among groups who already feel poorly served by the justice system. Second, equal opportunity: judicial office is a public career, and barriers to under-represented groups are unfair in themselves, whatever the effect on outcomes. Third, decision-making: life experience can shape how judges find facts, assess witnesses and frame legal questions, which feminist judgments projects explore; Hunter (2015), reviewing the research, finds the evidence of different outcomes mixed and dependent on context. Against this, judges are trained to apply the law impartially and do not 'represent' groups, and evidence that diversity changes outcomes is limited. The Constitutional Reform Act 2005 keeps merit as the test, with only an equal-merit tie-breaker.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the effect of Churchill v Merthyr Tydfil CBC [2023]?
options: Courts may order parties to engage in non-court dispute resolution if the order does not impair the essence of the right to a hearing, pursues a legitimate aim and is proportionate
Courts may never order parties to mediate
All civil claims must go to arbitration before trial
Mediation outcomes are binding court judgments
questions.why: Churchill held that courts have this power, treating Halsey's contrary remarks as obiter. 'Never' is the Halsey view that Churchill rejected. There is no general requirement of arbitration, which is a binding private adjudication chosen by agreement; this option confuses ADR in general with arbitration. Mediation produces a settlement agreement, not a court judgment, so treating its outcome as a judgment confuses mediation with adjudication.

questions.q: In a mediation, what is the role of the mediator?
options: To help the parties negotiate their own settlement without imposing a decision
To act as a judge in a court hearing
To decide the dispute and impose a binding result
To advise one party on the strength of its case
questions.why: A mediator is a neutral facilitator. Deciding and imposing a result describes an arbitrator or judge. Advising one side is the role of that party's lawyer. Mediation takes place outside the court's adjudication, even when ordered by a court.

questions.q: Evaluate the shift towards ADR in civil justice in England and Wales. (5 marks)
markScheme: Describes shift: Woolf/CPR; Halsey to Churchill; 2024 CPR amendments; small claims mediation
Benefits: cost, speed, party control, less adversarial
Concerns: power imbalance; privacy and lack of precedent/public norms (Genn); pressure to settle
Access to justice and constitutional role of courts (UNISON)
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer: Civil justice has moved from encouraging ADR to requiring it. The Woolf reforms and the Civil Procedure Rules 1998 encouraged settlement; Halsey (2004) refused to compel mediation, but Churchill (2023) held that courts may order parties to engage in ADR, and the 2024 CPR amendments built this into the overriding objective and costs rules. Small money claims are now referred to mediation automatically. ADR can be cheaper and faster and lets parties shape their own outcomes. But it can magnify power imbalances, it happens in private, and it does not produce public precedents; Genn argues that the decline of adjudication weakens the courts' role in declaring law. UNISON (2017) stresses that access to courts has public as well as private value. On balance, ADR is valuable as an option, but should not become a cheaper substitute that denies people a hearing.

questions.q: Which study showed that ranchers in Shasta County, California, settled disputes mainly through informal norms rather than formal law?
options: Ellickson, Order without Law (1991)
Griffiths, 'What is Legal Pluralism?' (1986)
Merry, 'Legal Pluralism' (1988)
Macaulay, 'Non-Contractual Relations in Business' (1963)
questions.why: Ellickson studied Shasta County. Macaulay studied how Wisconsin businesses used (and avoided) contract law, a related finding about a different group. Griffiths offered a theoretical definition of legal pluralism rather than a field study. Merry's article surveyed legal pluralism in colonial and modern societies rather than reporting a study of ranchers.

questions.q: Under English law, what is the legal status of a Beth Din decision in a commercial dispute where both parties agreed to arbitration?
options: It overrides English law for members of the community
It is binding because religious courts such as the Beth Din form part of the English court system
It can be enforced as an arbitration award under the Arbitration Act 1996, subject to that Act's safeguards
It has no legal effect at all
questions.why: Parties can choose arbitration, including by a religious tribunal, and the award is then enforceable under the 1996 Act. 'No legal effect' is the position of religious divorces granted by sharia councils, not of agreed arbitration. Religious tribunals cannot override English law: the award is enforced only within the limits the Act sets. They are private bodies, not part of the state's court system; their decisions bind only because the parties agreed to arbitrate.

questions.q: Distinguish 'weak' and 'strong' legal pluralism, giving an example of each. (4 marks)
markScheme: Weak/juristic: state legal system recognises and incorporates other normative orders (e.g. personal or religious law in some post-colonial states; arbitration by religious tribunals under the Arbitration Act 1996)
Strong: empirical coexistence of multiple orders regardless of state recognition
Example of strong: informal norms (Ellickson's ranchers; Macaulay's businesses; community religious councils)
Source: Griffiths (1986)
questions.modelAnswer: John Griffiths (1986) distinguished two senses. Weak, or juristic, pluralism exists when the state's legal system itself recognises other bodies of norms, for example applying religious personal law to different communities in some post-colonial states, or, in England, enforcing arbitration awards by religious tribunals under the Arbitration Act 1996. Strong pluralism is the social fact that several normative orders operate in the same field whatever the state says, such as the informal neighbourly norms of Ellickson's Shasta County ranchers or the business practices Macaulay described.

questions.q: Which statement about jury verdicts in England and Wales is correct?
options: Verdicts must always be unanimous
Juries must give written reasons for their verdict
A majority verdict of 10–2 may be accepted after at least two hours of deliberation
A simple majority of 7–5 is enough
questions.why: Juries Act 1974 s 17 allows 11–1 or 10–2 majorities after at least two hours. Unanimity is the starting point but not always required. Juries give no reasons, which is one criticism of them. A 7–5 majority is not permitted.

questions.q: What did the Lammy Review (2017) conclude about juries, drawing on Cheryl Thomas's research?
options: Jury verdicts did not differ for ethnic minority and white defendants, so juries were described as a success story
Juries systematically convicted ethnic minority defendants more often
Juries should be abolished for all either-way offences
All-white juries should be banned
questions.why: Lammy found the jury verdict stage was one point where ethnic minority defendants were not treated disproportionately. Systematic bias in convictions is the opposite of what the research found. Abolition for either-way offences was not Lammy's recommendation (later proposals to restrict the right to elect came from Sir Brian Leveson's Independent Review of the Criminal Courts). The review did not recommend banning all-white juries, since the evidence showed they did not deliver different results.

questions.q: Assess two arguments for and two against trial by jury. (5 marks)
markScheme: For: democratic participation and legitimacy (Devlin: 'lamp that shows that freedom lives')
For: community standards and check on oppressive prosecutions (Bushell's Case; Ponting)
Against: cost, delay and complexity, especially fraud; no reasons given
Against: risk of prejudice or tampering (CJA 2003 s 44)
Uses evidence (Thomas 2010; Lammy 2017) and reaches a view
questions.modelAnswer: Two arguments for juries: first, they involve ordinary citizens in criminal justice, which supports public confidence and legitimacy; Devlin called the jury 'the lamp that shows that freedom lives'. Second, juries apply community standards and can act as a check on oppressive laws or prosecutions, as in Ponting (1985), building on Bushell's Case (1670). Two arguments against: juries are slower and costlier than judges, especially in long, complex fraud trials, and they give no reasons, which makes errors hard to detect on appeal. They may also be prejudiced or tampered with, which is why s 44 of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 allows judge-only trials in tampering cases. On prejudice, however, Thomas's research (2010), relied on by the Lammy Review (2017), found no difference in jury verdicts by ethnicity, which weakens that criticism.

questions.q: Essay (in the style of the LL141 formative essay). 'Judges in England and Wales do not merely apply the law: they make it.' Discuss with reference to precedent and statutory interpretation.
markScheme: Declaratory theory vs law-making (Lord Reid's 'fairy tale')
Precedent: ratio/obiter, distinguishing, Practice Statement departures (Shivpuri, Jogee, Knauer); creative development (Donoghue v Stevenson; R v R)
Constraints: hierarchy (Young v Bristol Aeroplane), retrospectivity concerns, deference to Parliament
Statutory interpretation: literal/golden/mischief; purposive (Quintavalle); contextual primacy of text (R (O) 2022); limits
HRA s 3 as strong interpretive power (Ghaidan) and s 4 declaration as boundary
Comparative perspective: civil law codes; US Supreme Court overruling
Theory: Hart's open texture/discretion vs Dworkin's principles
Balanced conclusion: judges make law interstitially within institutional constraints
questions.modelAnswer:
The declaratory theory held that judges only discover pre-existing law. Lord Reid called this a 'fairy tale' (1972), and few now defend it. The better question is how, and within what limits, judges make law.

Through precedent, judges plainly create law. Donoghue v Stevenson (1932) established the modern law of negligence; R v R (1992) removed the marital rape exemption. The 1966 Practice Statement lets the highest court depart from its own decisions, as in Shivpuri (1986), overruling Anderton v Ryan only about a year after it was decided, and Jogee (2016), which corrected 30 years of complicity law. Even lower courts shape law through distinguishing, since the ratio of a case depends on how later courts characterise its material facts. Leggatt LJ's discussion in Youngsam (2019) shows that identifying a ratio involves judgement about how persuasive the earlier reasoning is.

But precedent also constrains. The Court of Appeal is bound by its own decisions except in the Young v Bristol Aeroplane situations, and lower courts must follow higher ones. Because judicial change is retrospective, courts are cautious where policy choices are better made by Parliament after consultation.

Statutory interpretation is supposedly the application of Parliament's words. Yet the choice of approach affects outcomes: the literal rule acquitted the defendant in Whiteley v Chappell, while the mischief rule convicted in Smith v Hughes. The modern purposive approach can extend statutes to new situations, as in Quintavalle (2003). In R (O) (2022) the Supreme Court stressed that the words in context are the primary source, a reminder that judges claim to be applying Parliament's choices. The strongest power is s 3 of the Human Rights Act 1998, under which Ghaidan (2004) read words in a way Parliament had not intended in 1977. The limit is s 4: where a compatible reading is impossible, judges must declare incompatibility rather than rewrite the statute.

Comparison helps. Civil law judges work from codes and are formally forbidden from laying down general rules, yet settled case law guides them in practice. The US Supreme Court openly overrules major precedents, making its law-making highly political. English judges sit between these models.

Theoretically, Hart saw judges as having discretion in the 'open texture' of rules, so they make law at the margins. Dworkin argued that judges find the answer that best fits and justifies existing principles, which is not unconstrained creation.

The statement is therefore true but incomplete. Judges in England and Wales do make law, sometimes boldly, but interstitially and within constraints of hierarchy, text and institutional deference to Parliament.

questions.q: Essay. 'Lay participation in legal decision-making is a democratic luxury that an overstretched justice system can no longer afford.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains lay participation: juries (Juries Act 1974), magistrates, tribunal lay members
Democratic and legitimacy arguments (Devlin; Bushell's Case; Ponting)
Evidence on fairness (Thomas 2010; Lammy Review 2017)
Costs, delays and backlog; complexity (fraud); jury tampering (CJA 2003 s 44)
Current reform: Courts and Tribunals Bill (removal of election; judge-only complex trials; bench division dropped); status at time of writing
Magistrates: low-cost lay justice but concerns on consistency/diversity
Links to due process and legitimacy of adjudication
Reasoned conclusion on proportionality of reforms
questions.modelAnswer:
Lay participation takes two main forms in England and Wales: juries in the Crown Court and lay magistrates, who decide the great majority of criminal cases. The statement suggests that the democratic value of lay involvement is outweighed by cost and delay. That claim needs testing against both principle and evidence.

The democratic case is strong. Bushell's Case (1670) established that jurors cannot be punished for their verdict, and juries have acted as a check on prosecutions seen as oppressive, as in Ponting (1985). Devlin described the jury as 'the lamp that shows that freedom lives'. Lay participation also brings community standards into decisions, for example in judging dishonesty, and supports public confidence.

Fairness is often questioned, but evidence supports juries. Cheryl Thomas's research (2010) found little evidence of unfairness by ethnicity in jury verdicts, and the Lammy Review (2017) called juries a success story because verdicts did not differ for ethnic minority and white defendants, even with all-white juries. That contrasts with disparities Lammy found at other stages of the criminal process.

The efficiency case against juries has gained force with Crown Court backlogs. Jury trials are longer and more expensive than judge-only trials, juries give no reasons, and long fraud trials place heavy demands on jurors. Judge-only trials are already possible where there is a real and present danger of jury tampering (Criminal Justice Act 2003, s 44; R v Twomey (2009)). The Courts and Tribunals Bill, before the House of Lords at the time of writing (October 2026), would remove the right of adult defendants to elect jury trial in either-way cases and introduce judge-only trials for certain complex and lengthy cases. A proposed Crown Court 'bench division', which would have tried some either-way offences without a jury, was removed during the Commons stages, but the core limits on jury trial remain.

Magistrates show that lay justice can also be cheap: they are unpaid volunteers. Concerns focus on consistency and diversity rather than cost.

Evaluation: the delays that justify reform are themselves a due process problem, because justice delayed harms victims and defendants. But delay has many causes, including court closures and limited sitting days, and reducing lay participation addresses only part of it. Removing the right to elect shifts power from defendants to the state, and judge-only trials lose the legitimacy that comes from community judgment.

Lay participation is therefore not a luxury: it carries real democratic and legitimacy value, supported by evidence of fairness. Targeted limits, for example in exceptionally complex cases, may be justified, but broad reductions risk solving a resourcing problem by weakening a constitutional safeguard.
